Voat is a pretty good, functional alternative to reddit. No argument there. I greatly admire the hands off approach of the admins, and the enhanced feature set, compared to that other website. That being said, voat is still susceptible to some of reddit's own inherent weaknesses. These weaknesses derive primarily, I believe, from voat being incorporated in the US, and its dependency on income. To put it simply, if voat isn't profitable, on a long enough timeline, it will cease to function. As well, voat is subject to the whims of the US government, and, as a centralized service, so is voat's user data. Additionally, the worst two problems I see affecting both voat and reddit are mod abuse and shilling/vote manipulation.

So, how do we defeat these weaknesses?

I've given a lot thought to this issue. Well, maybe that's giving myself more credit than I should. I'll say that I've daydreamed quite a bit about it, though. Here are some ideas I've had.

The short of my idea is a public forum, blending aspects of twitter, voat/reddit, 4chan, bit coin, and TOR.

So, imagine a twitter-esque application, that would allow reddit/voat-esque conversation threads derived from "tweets". The "tweets", or whatever we'd call them, would be organized according to their hashtag, as opposed to being submitted to subverses or subreddits. The hashtags would be devoid of mods, but the search results for a hashtag would or could be organized based on their vote count "hotness". The "hotness" could be calculated by a simple algorithm, based on up votes over time, providing as true a meritocracy as possible. I think this scheme would do well to prevent mod abuse, as there would be no mods.

But what if this forum were decentralized, and based on a peer to peer distribution system, the way bit coin and bit torrent are? Posts would be submitted to the forums' "message chain" and distributed amongst users the way transactions are submitted to bitcoin's block chain. This would prevent administrators from stepping in and removing conversations they don't agree with, because there would be no centralized administrators. To keep the "bock chain" from getting out of control in size, conversations would be truncated according to their age, sort of like how 4chan "has no memory". If remembering becomes a big deal at some point in the future, secondary services could be setup to fill that role, outside of what we're talking about here, anyway.

Now, what about shilling and vote manipulation? Here's where I think my idea gets a little crazy. We try to emulate bitcoin in this aspect, specifically bitcoin's proof of work feature. However, instead of mining for bitcoins, you're mining for karma, up to a certain limit. Then you distribute this karma by up voting posts you like, and down voting posts you don't like. Once you're out of karma, you have to wait until you've mined more. Now, I think this would be somewhat limiting, in as far as how much voting participation a user could expect, but that's the point. Users would be more stingy with their votes, naturally, and would have to rely more on their commenting abilities to voice their opinion. Not a bad thing, IMHO. Most importantly, shills would be severely handicapped in their ability to influence the flow of conversation. I'm not saying vote manipulation couldn't happen, I'm saying it would be a lot more difficult than just generating an army of accounts to do your bidding for you.

Now I'm going to get really crazy. I think posts should be submitted through a TOR-like round robin of encryption. Posts would be passed between the users mining for karma, shedding a layer of encryption through every stop, until, finally, being posted to the forum message chain. With the Snowden revelations, I don't think anyone really expects a modicum of privacy or anonymity these days, in as far as what is said on forum services like facebook, or twitter, or reddit, or even voat, for that matter. What we're saying is being watched, all the time. That has had a significant chilling effect on conversation, I think. I doubt many people truly feel free to voice their opinions, without fearing some sort of possible back lash for it, at least a little bit. When combined with the decentralized, admin-free paradigm of the service, providing a hardened level of anonymity would, I think, be a very attractive feature, especially to those disaffected by society or their government.

Now, having ideas is one thing, but there are a couple of things I've learned during my time on this Earth. One of them being that nobody gives a fuck about your ideas, even if they're good ones, if you're unable to put them in motion. I am actually a software developer, and I could gear myself towards making what I'm talking about a reality, if the idea does in fact have some credence to it. If not, why waste the energy?

So, tell me, how fucking stupid am I?

There are three constraints you need to consider at the beginning of any such project.

The first can be summarized as the "child porn problem". If your system can't remove CP, the people who build and run the system will be hunted down. If it can remove it, then you have to manage this mechanism so that it does not remove other things as well. This gets complicated when you appreciate that CP is not the only illegal content that you need to be concerned with, and that every nation has it's own ever-changing opinion about what is legal or not.

The second problem is money. Bandwidth, storage, and software development and maintenance are not free. Putting your message system into a blockchain does not magically make this problem go away. You can store fairly small amounts of data across a distributed network of home computers, but you won't be serving terabytes of image and music files to a global audience in a timely manner that way. It just won't scale. Furthermore, the maintenance demands are incessant no matter how well you build the original product.

The third? The biggest hurdle of all is that governments regulate all the existent communications media. Your internet posts go over phone lines and telecom cables. Even if you resorted to ham radio, even the RF frequencies are licensed and regulated. If the carriers won't carry you, you're sunk. Sure, you can encrypt your packets and slip some of them through, but your network will always be vulnerable to disruption and your users vulnerable to arrest.

If there was a feasible way to do it, the CP crowd would have done it long ago, and we'd all be buying our weed on the darknet.

Interesting idea and one I've been toying with myself. I'm choosing to ignore most points I'd have contention with to highlight just one big one: block chain usage.

Block chain size will be a problem here just as it is for bitcoin. They sorta gloss over the whole thing in the Twister white paper (which is similar to what you propose): https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7152

You can see some discussion of the issue here: https://github.com/miguelfreitas/twister-core/issues/90

For a less-technical and more bitcoin-centric treatment: http://www.ibtimes.com/bitcoins-big-problem-transaction-delays-renew-blockchain-debate-2330143

Basically, people are coming to realize that to process these very big block chains, you need some heavyweight centralized computing devices and this starts to defeat the decentralized promise of crypto-currencies. My general advice for anyone looking to block chains in their currently described form as the silver bullet to problems in developing decentralized computing solutions is "don't". Or at least if you're going to, you better start out by figuring out how you're going to prevent unbounded growth in your block chains. Failing that, you will just be treading down the exact same road as BitCoin (which isn't necessarily as nicely paved as some may think).
